title: Completing the square
keyIdea: Completing the square rewrites x² + bx + c as (x + p)² + q, where p = b/2 and q = c − p². It works because (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p², so you add p² to make a perfect square and take it away again. In this form you can read off the turning point (−p, q), see that the minimum value is q, and solve the equation by taking square roots.

kid: Picture x² + 6x as tiles: one big x by x square and six thin x strips. Put 3 strips down the right side and 3 along the bottom. Now it is nearly a square with side x + 3. Only a 3 by 3 corner is missing. That corner is 9 small squares.

x² + 6x + 2 only has 2 small squares. Use them in the corner and borrow 7 more. The shape is now (x + 3)². But you borrowed 7, so you must take 7 away. That gives x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7. Check it: (x + 3)² is x² + 6x + 9, and 9 − 7 = 2.

The rule is short. Halve the number in front of x to get p, and keep its sign. Then take p² away from the number on the end. For x² − 8x + 3, half of −8 is −4. So it is (x − 4)² − 16 + 3, which is (x − 4)² − 13.

Why is this useful? A square can never be less than 0. So (x − 2)² + 3 is smallest when the bracket is 0, at x = 2, and the smallest value is 3. The graph's turning point is (2, 3). You can also solve equations: (x + 3)² = 7 gives x + 3 = √7 or −√7, so x = −3 ± √7.
adult: This lesson covers the GCSE Mathematics content in England on completing the square (Higher tier). Learners write x² + bx + c in the form (x + p)² + q, use it to find turning points, and solve quadratic equations. It also matches the US Common Core standards A-SSE.B.3b (complete the square to reveal the maximum or minimum value) and A-REI.B.4a (use completing the square to transform an equation).

Key terms: quadratic expression, perfect square, completing the square, completed-square form (x + p)² + q, turning point (vertex), minimum value, line of symmetry x = −p, and the ± square root. The identity behind it is (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p², so p = b/2. Cases where the x² term has a number in front, such as 2x² + 12x + 1, are a next step and are not covered here.

Common mistakes: using b instead of b/2, so x² + 8x becomes (x + 8)². Forgetting to subtract p², so q is left as c. Giving p the wrong sign, or reading the turning point of (x + 5)² − 2 as (5, −2) instead of (−5, −2). Swapping the coordinates of the turning point. Taking only the positive square root when solving, which loses one of the two solutions.

In the lab the learner splits six x-strips round an x² tile to see the 3 × 3 gap, then fills the gap from the +2 and borrows 7. They pick p for three quadratics, with traps for b, −b/2 and p². Then they slide along two parabolas to mark the turning point, and choose each line of a solution of x² + 6x + 2 = 0.

familyTip: Ask your learner for the smallest value of x² − 4x + 7 without drawing a graph. Then try a few numbers together: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 give 7, 4, 3, 4 and 7. Ask why 3 is the smallest, and why the values are the same on both sides of x = 2.

practice.prompt: Write x² + {=2*k}x + 1 as (x + p)² + q. What is p?
practice.hint: p is half of the number in front of x: half of {=2*k}.
practice.explain: Half of {=2*k} is {k}, so p = {k} and x² + {=2*k}x + 1 = (x + {k})² + 1 − {=k*k}.

practice.prompt: What is the turning point of y = (x + 5)² − 2?
practice.hint: The square is 0 when x + 5 = 0. What is y there?
practice.explain: (x + 5)² = 0 when x = −5, and then y = −2. So the turning point is (−5, −2). The sign inside the bracket flips for the x-coordinate.
x − 1 = 3 or x − 1 = −3, so x = 4 or x = −2. Taking only the positive root loses x = −2.

pool.hint: Halve 8 for p, then take p² away from 5.
pool.explain: Half of 8 is 4, and (x + 4)² = x² + 8x + 16. So x² + 8x + 5 = (x + 4)² − 16 + 5 = (x + 4)² − 11.

pool.prompt: What is the minimum value of x² − 4x + 7?
pool.hint: Complete the square first: half of −4 is −2.
pool.explain: x² − 4x + 7 = (x − 2)² + 3. The square is never negative, so the smallest value is 3, at x = 2.

pool.prompt: y = x² − {=2*k}x + 20. What is the x-coordinate of its turning point?
pool.hint: Complete the square: half of −{=2*k} is −{k}, so the bracket is (x − {k}).
pool.explain: y = (x − {k})² + 20 − {=k*k}. The bracket is 0 when x = {k}, so the turning point has x-coordinate {k}.

pool.prompt: x² + {=2*k}x + 30 has a minimum value. What is it?
pool.hint: Write it as (x + {k})² + q, then q is the minimum.
pool.explain: x² + {=2*k}x + 30 = (x + {k})² + 30 − {=k*k}, so the minimum value is {=30-k*k}, reached at x = −{k}.

pool.prompt: Solve x² + 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square.
pool.hint: x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7. Set that to 0 and isolate the square.
pool.explain: (x + 3)² = 7, so x + 3 = ±√7 and x = −3 ± √7 (about −0.35 or −5.65). Both roots count.

pool.hint: (x − 5)² = x² − 10x + 25. What do you add to 25 to get 30?
pool.explain: q = 30 − 25 = 5. Subtract p², do not add it, and keep the sign of the result.

pool.prompt: Why does completing the square tell you the minimum of x² + bx + c?
choices: (x + p)² is never negative, so the expression is smallest when the bracket is 0
pool.hint: What is the smallest value a square can take?
pool.explain: A square is 0 or more, so (x + p)² + q is at least q, and equals q when x = −p. That is the turning point (−p, q).
